title: A decade on from the Higher Education & Research Act (HERA), it’s time for the new sector champions to arise

The post A decade on from the Higher Education & Research Act (HERA), it’s time for the new sector champions to arise  appeared first on HEPI.
full_text:
Today’s blog was kindly authored by Daniel Gilbert. He was Special Adviser to Jo Johnson, former Minister for Universities and Science and is now a Partner at consultancy Shearwater Global.

Yesterday’s HEPI / AHEP / TechnologyOne webinar on ‘Invest now or pay later? The future of professional services in higher education’ is available to watch on our YouTube channel.

Higher education is in a bind. Our universities are renowned globally, driving billions in exports and powering world-class research. Yet listen to the domestic conversation – as I did recently at the party conferences – and you hear a jarringly different story: a narrative that too often characterises universities as part of the problem in British society, rather than a solution to our challenges.

There are, without doubt, some home truths that we need to confront. The most pressing of these is related to the jobs market, with graduates making up 15% of the 1 million NEETs. But it is easy in such a climate to lose sight of a basic truism. No ambitious country anywhere in the world is actively looking to shrink its university sector. As we approach the tenth anniversary of the Higher Education and Research Act (HERA) – the legislation that shaped the regulation of the sector as it exists today – it is a timely moment to reflect on why the reforms came about, what they achieved, and what should come next.

Unfinished business from the Coalition era

First, a personal recollection. Ten years ago, winding back through several machinery of government changes, I was a newly-minted Special Adviser for Jo Johnson in the former Department for Business, Innovation & Skills. We arrived in the department with a small majority, unshackled from the constraints of coalition, and a clear vision set out in the manifesto which Jo had responsibility for drafting:

We will ensure that universities deliver the best possible value for money to students: we will introduce a framework to recognise universities offering the highest teaching quality; encourage universities to offer more two-year courses; and require more data to be openly available to potential students so that they can make decisions informed by the career paths of past graduates.

We will maintain our universities’ reputation for world-class research and academic excellence. Through the Nurse Review of research councils, we will seek to ensure that the UK continues to support world-leading science, and invests public money in the best possible way.

The logic was twofold. The increase in tuition fees and removal of the student numbers cap required a new approach – one that shifted away from a funding council model that carved up grants, and towards a regulatory framework that incentivised outcomes. What followed was the Office for Students and Teaching Excellence Framework.

On the research side, budgetary protection was a rare good news story for the Conservative government, but there was a nagging feeling that the sum of the parts added up to less than the whole. This led firstly to a planned research council merger (“Research UK”) and then to a supercharged UKRI, encompassing the dual support system and Innovate UK. For the Treasury, I sensed this was partly a tidying-up exercise. From a Special Adviser’s perspective, it was an opportunity to spend less time vetting a plethora of council board vacancies when attention should be on a joined-up research strategy.

Legislation was never guaranteed – we had to make the case

HERA may have had manifesto cover, but a slot on the parliamentary calendar was not guaranteed. We were acutely aware that an HE bill was a political risk. It would be a target for opposition amendments and the proposals were never likely to inspire Conservative backbench enthusiasm. We still needed top-tier political consent.

There was a scenario in which HERA never happened, and HEFCE survived. The breakdown in relations between the department and the funding council was an open secret at the time. I remember it being difficult to see something as basic as HEFCE’s media grid. As a backstop exercise, officials had scoped the non-legislative means of achieving similar policy ends. An ambitious HEFCE could have saved itself by using its existing powers in a more creative way. But in practice that was only ever an incomplete option and would have required consistent ministerial direction. So we consulted first, taking care not to reveal our hand on legislation, while making the case for a bill internally.

From green paper to white paper: success as a knowledge economy

The title we chose for the November 2015 green paper sent a clear signal about our priorities: Fulfilling Our Potential: Teaching Excellence, Social Mobility and Student Choice. In the language of the Cameron government of the time:

These proposals reflect our mission as a One Nation Government to ensure everyone from all backgrounds can reach their full potential.

That document was careful to avoid committing to a bill. Over that Christmas, the case for a legislative slot was made behind the scenes both to the Prime Minister and Chancellor, aligning HERA to the Treasury’s long-term economic plan and the urgent productivity challenge. It was a lesson in the art of political weather-making watching Jo Johnson at work. At a time when politicians are so often denigrated, the last Conservative Government benefitted from a number of highly capable ministers covering education. It is fair to say that HERA could not have happened without Jo’s vision and determination – not least in the midst of an EU referendum and change of Prime Minister.

With political backing, the parliamentary counsel got drafting. To the surprise of the sector, a bill was ready immediately after the Queen’s Speech of May 2016. I had taken my laptop to a now-closed Café Rouge to finesse the white paper’s foreword and brainstorm ideas for the title. There was a quiet part of me that was pleased with the Blairite overtones: Success as a knowledge economy. You can hardly imagine a politician embracing that phrase now. The opening two pages are still worth reading a decade on. They demonstrate the clarity of the vision – and how we tried a decade ago to get ahead of issues that still rankle now:

If we are to continue to succeed as a knowledge economy…we cannot stand still, nor take for granted our universities’ enviable global reputation and position at the top of league tables. We must ensure that the system is also fulfilling its potential and delivering good value for students, for employers and for the taxpayers who underwrite it.

Legacy – TEF comes of age

The HERA settlement has proved remarkably durable. Successive governments of different political stripes have maintained its core pillars. Several changes of governments later, it is notable that the OfS is clearly doubling down on the TEF in its consultation on the future quality system.

If you look at the full span of what happened in those few years (not just HERA itself), then a picture emerges of a remarkably prescient agenda. The OfS and TEF were explicitly about value for money and good graduate outcomes. The legislation for publishing Longitudinal Educational Outcomes data established a means to link student loans to HMRC employment data. The first inflation-linked increase in tuition fees, which took place in 2017, was a financial sustainability measure, sadly not repeated for around a decade. The launch of earn-as-you-learn degree apprenticeships began to break down HE / FE barriers and foreshadowed the Lifelong Learning Entitlement. If HERA hadn’t been introduced a decade ago, a government today would need to create it.

The most contentious elements related to market entry. We were keen to encourage new providers like NMITE to bring something distinctive to the market. Given everything that’s happened since, it is no surprise that the Post-16 Education and Skills White Paper focuses on collaboration and financial sustainability rather than market opening. But the predicament the sector finds itself in today was a consequence of what came later. In reality, financial stability was integral to the HERA approach. The “English Votes for English Laws” procedure (known as EVEL and now rescinded) was used in the Commons to uprate fees in 2016. Thereafter, income was allowed to decline while the international student market remained restricted, before being liberated, and then restricted once more.

I have never bought the argument that liberalisation and quality were opposing bedfellows. The OfS was always intended as a quality booster, and we’ve seen in its new leadership – Directors of Higher Education in BIS a decade ago – a determination to tackle “pockets of poor provision” within the HERA framework. Their latest proposals can be summarised as TEF with Teeth: adding new post-study metrics on use of skills and earnings, and using TEF ratings to shape student recruitment numbers. Where there will be some debate is on restricting access to DAPs. Whatever the outcome, it would be a shame if we ended up with a system that made it harder to acquire DAPs but did not apply equal emphasis on encouraging innovation in the system.

With the benefit of hindsight, we could have done more on innovation

Promoting innovation was always a key plank of the HERA reforms. We only scratched the surface of what this could mean in terms of teaching and learning. With hindsight, more could have been done to build capacity in new institutions and encourage uptake of accelerated degrees. In practice, there was little fiscal wiggle room at the time.

English devolution has also blossomed in the decade since HERA. Universities have responded with bigger thinking on their civic contribution, but the system itself offers few formal incentives for this. If HERA were before Parliament today, I expect MPs and Peers would want to look at regional collaboration and skills planning as part of the general duties of the OfS. How soon this happens depends on whether the new government follows through on the proposal to legislate for annual fee indexation. (As a side note in these heady Burnham days, there was an alternative universe in which we based the OfS in Manchester, the heart of the Northern Powerhouse. It was discussed at the time, but the cost and expertise in HEFCE made that too difficult.)

Where the sector must urgently assert itself is in embracing the skills agenda and dismantling the unhelpful binary of higher versus further education. We need both political and sectoral leadership to change the public conversation about higher education. Visit institutions in any part of the country and you’ll find university departments producing nurses and social workers, teachers and engineers, pharmacists and physiotherapists. A substantial proportion of higher education is already technical and professional, and some of that HE is delivered in FE settings. The HE-scepticism that I heard at events across the party conferences is not based on reality. It is a false caricature that eats away at the sector’s reputation.

Was 2016 the high-point of political sponsorship of HE?

A decade on from HERA, we are at another turning point for the sector, with new leadership at the Office for Students and a new funding strategy at UKRI. We are also at a high point of external scrutiny of what universities are for.

It’s worth remembering that the HERA reforms were controversial at the time. There was criticism about the marketisation of higher education and fears about political interference in the research base. In hindsight, however, that was probably the high-point of political sponsorship of HE. Today, whichever party spokesperson you talk to, you get the faint impression that pride in our higher education sector can only be muttered awkwardly and in hushed tones. That’s the part that’s got to change. Whether it’s innovative new providers or ancient research-intensive institutions, higher education is a huge national asset. Ten years on from HERA, it’s time for the HE heroes to emerge.

title: Survey: Student Success Leaders Weigh In Ahead of 2027
summary:
Survey: Student Success Leaders Weigh In Ahead of 2027 colleen.flaherty Thu, 11/12/2026 - 03:00 AM Byline(s) IHE Staff Survey: Student Success Leaders Weigh In Ahead of 2027
colleen.flaherty Thu, 11/12/2026 - 03:00 AM
Byline(s)
IHE Staff
full_text:
Student success administrators are dealing with capacity issues and persistent challenges, finds Inside Higher Ed’s third annual Survey of College and University Student Success Administrators with Hanover Research, out today. They’re also confident in their institution’s core product and hopeful that artificial intelligence can meaningfully improve the student experience, even as many haven’t yet seen student-facing gains. Check out our reporting on that here. And check out our reporting on the survey’s findings on digital betting here.

More on the survey: Insufficient financial aid or needing to work long hours to cover living costs is the leading challenge to academic success and persistence, cited by 72 percent of respondents. Mental and behavioral health challenges rank second (55 percent), followed by gaps in academic preparation (47 percent) and basic needs insecurity (33 percent). For community college leaders, basic needs insecurity is nearly as prominent as financial constraints (65 percent versus 67 percent, respectively).

On career preparation, some 83 percent of student success administrators agree that their institution’s students earn the credentials needed to enter their chosen fields. Overall confidence is lower in students’ experiential learning preparation, however (69 percent, though this increases to 81 percent among private nonprofit institutional leaders), and in their ability to articulate specific skills to employers (61 percent). Embedding experiential learning into coursework (58 percent), helping students articulate their skills (46 percent) and expanding industry partnerships for internships and direct-hire opportunities (45 percent) are respondents’ top career-readiness priorities. Just 31 percent say postgraduate outcomes information is easily accessible and clearly communicated through official channels (similar to 2025’s 24 percent).

Nine in 10 leaders rate their connection with the students they serve as good or excellent; 81 percent rate their overall job satisfaction highly. A much smaller share—47 percent rate—rate their career-advancement opportunities highly. In write-in responses about the single most effective change their institution could make to boost student success, leaders highlight more resources, proactive support, coordination and institutional focus on outcomes. Technology, including AI, is framed as a means to support these goals, not an end in itself.

title: The Singularity, Black October and Other Lessons for Higher Education
summary:
The Singularity, Black October and Other Lessons for Higher Education mnelson@upcea.edu Thu, 11/12/2026 - 03:00 AM What happens when the exponential growth graph of a technology approaches the point at which it begins to go vertical? That is just where we are in the implementation of agentic AI. Byline(s) Ray Schroeder The Singularity, Black October and Other Lessons for Higher Education
mnelson@upcea.edu Thu, 11/12/2026 - 03:00 AM

What happens when the exponential growth graph of a technology approaches the point at which it begins to go vertical? That is just where we are in the implementation of agentic AI.

Byline(s)
Ray Schroeder
full_text:
Since the release of ChatGPT 3.5 just four years ago this month, we have experienced a steady to ever-increasing rate of improvement in generative artificial intelligence. Most notably, however, we have experienced some milestones in the past year or two, such as the advent of agentic AI in which semi- to fully autonomous agents endowed with AI capabilities can make changes with relatively little direction from humans.

While the early conceptual roots of agentic AI date back to the 1940s, it wasn’t until late 2024 that “Anthropic introduced the Model Context Protocol (MCP), an open-source framework intended to standardize the way agents integrate and share data with external tools, systems and data sources. The following year, IBM introduced the Agent Communication Protocol (ACP), which aimed to standardize the way agents communicate with one another. ACP later merged with Google’s Agent2Agent (A2A) protocol under the Linux Foundation.”

Change is now happening very rapidly as the capabilities of agentic artificial intelligence accelerate into a near-vertical graph of capabilities day by day, month by month and year by year. We are seeing the beginnings of recursive self-improvement, which Anthropic defines as “a process where an artificial intelligence system iteratively analyzes, redesigns and builds a more capable version of itself, creating a feedback loop that accelerates future development.”

Most Popular

Notably, as MIT Technology Review points out, “some futurists such as Ray Kurzweil have hypothesized that we will someday soon pass through a Singularity—that is, a time period of rapid technological change beyond which we cannot envision the future of society. Most visions of this Singularity focus on the creation of machines intelligent enough to devise machines even more intelligent than themselves, and so forth recursively, thus launching a positive feedback loop of intelligence amplification.”

Anthropic goes on to say, “These trends have huge implications. AI that can build itself would be a major development in the history of technology—one that could bring enormous good for the world in science, healthcare and beyond.” This is expected with well-funded scaling of resources and technologies across the industry of AI, given that enough resources such as computing power and an ever-increasing font of data results in the accelerating capabilities that we are seeing today. In our current situation, the growth is further reinforced by enabling very efficient recursive self-improvement, where the resulting AI is applied to creating further advancements in itself.

In “When AI Builds Itself,” Anthropic foreshadows the future in which recursive self-improvement accelerates to the extent that humans are challenged to keep up with understanding and making sense out of the new developments: “The technical trends discussed in this piece suggest that AI systems are going to become much more capable in coming years. These trends have huge implications. But full recursive self-improvement also might increase the risks of humans losing control over AI systems. If systems are capable of fully building their own successors, the ways we secure them, monitor them and shape their behavior all grow much more important."

This came to the fore in the middle of October, when agentic AI from OpenAI uncovered vulnerabilities in a common software program used for programs running on the internet, PHP. The internet got the wake-up call that cybersecurity experts and AI researchers had been warning about for months. As Miriam Waldvogel and Gerrit De Vynck reported for The Washington Post, a research firm disclosed that a programming language undergirding 70 percent of websites on the internet had a critical security issue.

The bug was found as part of an initiative by OpenAI to uncover software vulnerabilities with new AI models. (The Washington Post has a content partnership with OpenAI.) These vulnerabilities dated back to versions of the software that had not installed security patches. The incident was dubbed “Black October” to mark the beginning of a period in which advanced AI software is expected to be used by hackers and other malicious parties to uncover software vulnerabilities.

Then, on Oct. 29, CBS News reported that the cryptocurrency exchange Binance was hit by a historic cyberattack where hackers, apparently using AI, stole between $6.3 billion and $6.43 billion in digital assets. This incident is widely cited as the largest cryptocurrency theft—and potentially the largest single heist of any kind—in human history. It is attributed to TraderTraitor hackers from North Korea, who may have been using a host of AI agents.

The CEO of OpenAI, Sam Altman, just issued his scariest warning yet—that Black October was only the beginning of AI finding vulnerabilities in software online. He noted that “people did not intuit the exponential.” That is, people did not comprehend that the abilities of AI are escalating along an exponential curve. The problem may disrupt huge numbers of sites, both large and small, for the next year and a half. Altman says, “I no longer believe we are going to patch all of the bugs; we are going to have to completely switch the defense model for a new kind of defense shield.”

Meanwhile, it is important that we in higher education realize that we have entered a new era of AI-enabled attacks on security at our institutions. The messages are not new, but the likelihood of attack has increased. GPT-6 Astra Light recommends these five practical lessons:

Know what you operate—and patch rapidly. Maintain a campuswide inventory of PHP-based websites and applications, including departmental systems. PHP2Shell illustrates why application logins cannot compensate for vulnerabilities in the underlying software.

Protect privileged devices and approval processes. Reporting on Binance points to a compromised laptop with access to transaction-approval infrastructure. Universities should tightly restrict administrative access and require independent approval for sensitive financial and system changes.

Limit the damage one compromise can cause. Separate public websites, research systems, student records and financial operations; give users, applications and AI agents only the permissions they require.

Prepare to respond in minutes. Much of the Binance theft reportedly occurred within about 20 minutes. Universities need continuous monitoring, rapid credential revocation and rehearsed authority to isolate compromised systems.

Make cybersecurity an institutional responsibility. Assign clear ownership, enforce standards across decentralized units and regularly test incident response and recovery.

The central lesson is that trusted software, devices and authorized workflows can all become entry points. Security must include verification, containment and rapid response.

October 2026 marked the beginning of the predicted era of the emerging singularity, in which the agentic systems are capable of fully building their own successors that have capabilities that we may not fully understand in advance of their release and that those persons of malicious intent may utilize. Are you in a position that you might support or lead a comprehensive initiative at your institution to ensure your students, faculty and staff as well as valuable assets are best protected?

title: Minister’s office said contractor should handle CFMEU or lose work in Victoria, Big Build inquiry hears
summary:
Royal commission also hears from construction company employee who says workers were ‘fearful’ of union

  • Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

A major contractor on a troubled Victorian rail project shut down by union officials was warned that the minister’s office felt it would not “have any more work” in the state if it did not resolve the industrial dispute, a royal commission has heard.

The royal commission into the integrity of major public and civil infrastructure construction projects in Victoria heard from a Victorian Infrastructure Delivery Authority (Vida) official for the first time on Friday.

Continue reading...
full_text:
A major contractor on a troubled Victorian rail project shut down by union officials was warned that the minister’s office felt it would not “have any more work” in the state if it did not resolve the industrial dispute, a royal commission has heard.

The royal commission into the integrity of major public and civil infrastructure construction projects in Victoria heard from a Victorian Infrastructure Delivery Authority (Vida) official for the first time on Friday.

Vida was strongly criticised by counsel assisting the commission, Chris Young KC, on Thursday for its failure to disclose relevant evidence in a timely manner to the investigation.

The commission’s November public hearings, which are set to run until 20 November, are focusing on a 2022 level crossing removal project at Gap Road in Sunbury.

The commission previously heard that Construction, Forestry and Maritime Employees Union (CFMEU) officials shut down the site because of purported safety concerns, only for them to allow it to continue after two of their own health and safety representatives were appointed, and the project changed its traffic and labour hire companies to CFMEU-aligned firms.

Peter Wilkinson, a former Vida official who is now the executive general manager of the Suburban Rail Loop authority and a civil engineer, said that at the height of an industrial dispute at Gap Road he spoke about the need for work to resume on the project with Evan Tattersall, his manager at Vida.

He said Tattersall told him on either 6 or 7 June 2022 that he had discussed the issue with the minister’s office, and Wilkinson assumed that meant the office of the then-minister for transport infrastructure, Jacinta Allan.

Tattersall told him, Wilkinson said, “that if they can’t handle the industrial [relations] in Victoria, they can’t have any more work”.

Tattersall was referring to the contractors on the site, John Holland and CPB Constructions, Wilkinson said.

Wilkinson said he was aware at the time that the contractors were tendering for the airport rail, another major state government funded infrastructure project, but that he did not know if the minister’s office also knew this.

Wilkinson said Tattersall did not tell him what he should do with the information from the minister’s office, but he passed it on to Joe Aygur, the general manager of the Rail Network Alliance involved in the project’s delivery.

Aygur told the commission about the warning on Tuesday.

When asked by Young why no record of his conversation with Tattersall existed, Wilkinson said “probably one reason is that it was moving very quickly, so it was conversation that we had to keep it moving, rather than there being a need to formally record it.”

Wilkinson was also asked about a meeting scheduled in Allan’s parliament house office for 5pm on 7 June 2022 – the day work recommenced at Gap Road.

He was listed as an optional attendee on an online invite for the meeting, but said he could not recall if he attended.

The commission also heard on Friday from Stephen Villella, who worked for CPD Constructions and was the delivery director at the site, about the meeting at the union headquarters that ultimately ended the dispute.

He said it had been “extremely galling” for construction company officials to have to “bend the knee” by meeting with the CFMEU to resolve the matter.

Villella said none of the safety concerns raised by the union were serious enough to force work to stop at the site.

Workers on the project were fearful of the CFMEU and would stay in the lunchroom for long periods once they started to attend.

“They didn’t want to come [to work] at all,” Villella said.

“They were fearful of what would happen to them organisationally and individually if they did.”

Villella said he disagreed with evidence given early in the week by a former CFMEU organiser Paul Tzimas about those on site choosing not to work, saying they were heavily pressured by union officials.

Villella said that in the meeting with the CFMEU, a union organiser Joe Myles suggested collaborating would assist in winning future tenders such as the Melbourne airport rail project.

He said Myles also suggested he had direct lines to Allan’s office.

Villella said he was not surprised by Myles’ claim about having communication to the ministers office, as he had seen what had happened to the industry over the past 10 years.

Villella said Myles left abruptly in the first half of the about 30 minute meeting, which he said felt like a snub.

But he rejected a suggestion by counsel for Myles that it was not the union official, but rather Tzimas, who raised the list of union demands for the Gap Road project.

After construction managers agreed to the demands, work on the site resumed as normal.

“Amazingly, all our safety issues ceased,” Villella said.

Chris Carr SC, senior counsel assisting the commission, said that after the rebuke issued by Young on Thursday to Vida, he was “happy to report there has been substantial production of highly relevant material overnight”.

He said that production had led to several lines of inquiry, which meant the commission was unlikely to hear from witnesses again until Tuesday.

title: Abdul El-Sayed on Democratic leadership, health care access and inspiring a new generation
summary: The new Democratic senators are in Washington for orientation and are already facing tough questions about how they plan to govern. One is Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan, the first Muslim elected to the Senate. His win came after a hard-fought race marked by outside spending and attacks on his name and his faith. Amna Nawaz sat down with El-Sayed to discuss how he hopes to shake up Washington.
full_text:
Amna Nawaz:

The new wave of Democratic senators are in Washington this week for orientation and are already facing tough questions about how they plan to govern and who they'd like to lead their party. One of them is Abdul El-Sayed from Michigan. His win came after a hard-fought race marked by record outside spending and harsh attacks on his name and his faith. He will be the first Muslim ever elected to the US Senate. And Senator elect Abdul El-Sayed joins me now. Welcome. Thanks for being here.

Abdul El-Sayed:

Thank you so much for having me.

Amna Nawaz:

Congratulations on your win. You're here for orientation now. You've been a few days in Washington meeting new lawmakers. What's it been like? What surprised you most?

Abdul El-Sayed:

We've been thoroughly disoriented. No. You know, honestly, so much of the way that our politics are transacted make you think that these people hate each other in person. And the number of Republican future colleagues who've reached out talking about things that they want to work on together, has really been quite surprising.

Amna Nawaz:

That's already been happening?

Abdul El-Sayed:

Already been happening. And I don't know if it's just because too much of the way we do politics is about this sort of inside versus outside approach uh where um they make our politics purposely look like it's a food fight or it's because they're reading the tea leaves about the failure of Trump and Trumpism and folks are looking for partners to actually address some of the biggest challenges that they face. But you know I think the the way to read this election outcome is not as a mandate for Democrats. It is as a thorough repudiation for Trump and Trumpism with the opportunity for Democrats to earn their mandate over the next two years. And my hope is that Republicans see the opportunity to start addressing the failures of the war in Iran, the failures of this tariff policy uh and the impending doom that is going to come if these Medicaid cuts actually take hold in January.

Amna Nawaz:

Can you tell us who's been reaching out and what they want to work on?

Abdul El-Sayed:

I keep private conversations private, but I will tell you that they are Republican colleagues who had less than nice things to say about me during the campaign.

Amna Nawaz:

Maybe next time you come back, we'll get some more details on progress.

Abdul El-Sayed:

Perhaps we'll talk about legislation we work on together.

Amna Nawaz:

One of the first big decisions you're going to have to make is who will lead the Democrats in the Senate. You have acknowledged the work and the leadership of Chuck Schumer helping to secure these really big historic Senate wins. But you have called for Senator Chris Van Holland to be the next majority leader for the Senate Democrats. Why are you backing him?

Abdul El-Sayed:

Let me just start by saying that Senator Schumer and I worked very well together through the course of the general election. You know, we did not see eye to eye in the primary. He specifically supported my primary opponent, but you know, he understood the need to win Michigan. And he and the institutions that he leads came through in a big way uh to make sure that we were able to secure our uh our victory. That said, this is a moment where we need to pivot from the past into the future. You know, you've got this crop of freshman senators that hail from different parts of the country, parts of the country we didn't know, would elect a Democratic senator. And almost all of us came in saying that we needed to take a fresh approach, a new approach to governing.

Amna Nawaz:

You think Van Holland is a fresh approach? mean, he's been in Congress since early 2000.

Abdul El-Sayed:

If you're going to elect a leader, you want somebody who knows their way around the Senate. You know, he's led the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee. He has been a part of some of the most important legislation that has been passed. So he knows how to move a bill. He knows how to engage with his colleagues. He understands the caucus in a new and unique way. But at the same time, he takes a new approach. He's willing to take risks. For one, you know, when he chose to fly to El Salvador uh to meet with Kilmar Abrego Garcia, that was a real risk. When he chose to go to the Rafa crossing, that was a real risk. And he's shown his willingness to take those risks. And so, I just think he is somebody who both combines the understanding of the United States Senate as an institution, as a body, the processes of the Senate with the willingness to lead forward uh and to take some real risks.

Amna Nawaz:

Let's talk about what you want to do on that legislation front. You said one of the priorities is to reverse those Medicaid cuts. We know the new work requirements go into effect January 1st, but a repeal bill is likely going to face a veto from President Trump. You do not have 60 votes in the Senate to override it. So what is the plan to get that done?

Abdul El-Sayed:

Well, let's just think about what Medicaid cuts are going to do. When Medicaid gets cut, it doesn't just affect people on Medicaid because folks still get sick. So, now they're going to get health care when it's the most expensive, usually in an emergency room. So, what happens to those hospitals? Well, they're now facing costs that they can't bear. It's a big reason why it putting a lot of rural hospitals and health care centers in real danger of shutting down.

Amna Nawaz:

So, can you repeal these cuts?

Abdul El-Sayed:

But here's the point I'm making. If you are a senator from a state that is predominantly rural and because of the structure of the United States Senate, a lot of our senators disproportionately come from rural states on the other side of the aisle. So now you're looking at the potential collapse of your entire health care system in a state like Wyoming, in a state like Idaho, in a state like Montana, in a state like the Dakotas. And there's a real opportunity for us to say maybe we should not do that. And your electorate is probably looking at Trump and Trumpism and saying, "Yeah, I don't know about that." And if there's still something you can save from that big, ugly bill, maybe this is the opportunity to do it. So, I would not be surprised if we put a clean bill on the if we put a clean bill out there. I would not be surprised if we were able to get a lot of Republicans on board, maybe even a veto proof majority.

Amna Nawaz:

Medicare for all is a big part of your platform as well. And you've said recently that you are willing to call it "Trumpcare for All" if that helps to get the president on board. Is that a serious offer?

Abdul El-Sayed:

Yeah, I mean look, I don't care what we call it. I ran to get people healthcare. I really don't care what the name is. I want you to think about this. We are the richest, most powerful country in the world. And the idea that you cannot afford healthcare in this country. The idea that the collective medical debt is greater than the GDP of half the states in this country is insane. And meanwhile, you've got a president who's fighting a war. So, I'm just saying, hey, you did some dumb stuff. This would actually be a smart thing. And it seems like you like to put your name on things. So, why don't you put your name on the program that could finally address the unmet promise of America once and for all? It is the biggest affordability issue in America right now. We can solve it.

Amna Nawaz:

I just want to clarify, you've not been in touch with the president directly since you've won, have you?

Abdul El-Sayed:

I have not, but I communicate to him in the same way everybody communicates to him and he communicates to everybody else, which is on social media, apparently. So, Donald, if you're watching, let's do it.

Amna Nawaz:

So, in the last couple of weeks, we've seen the president name Steven Miller as his chief of staff. You've seen House Republicans name Jim Jordan as their next leader. You've seen the DOJ threaten Democratic lawmakers who will engage in oversight of the administration. What do you expect to see from the Trump administration in these next two years?

Abdul El-Sayed:

So, he said he wants to work with Democrats. I take everybody's claims on good faith and then when you look at where House Republicans have gone in choosing Jim Jordan as their minority leader, you look at what he's chosen in Stephen Miller as his White House chief of staff. It seems like the actions don't quite match the statements. You know, at the end of the day, this is a White House we're going to have to figure out how to engage with.

Amna Nawaz:

Can you work with this White House? Can you work with Stephen Miller?

Abdul El-Sayed:

That's a choice Stephen Miller is gonna have to make.

Amna Nawaz:

Your win in Michigan was nothing if not dramatic. Besides making history in someone with your faith joining the Senate, you overcame your primary rival, Haley Stevens, endorsing your Republican opponent at the last minute and you still won by seven points. Have you talked to Haley Stevens since then or heard from her since your win?

Abdul El-Sayed:

No, I'm more focused on leading for Michigan.

Amna Nawaz:

Do you anticipate speaking with her? And the reason I ask is because Democrats say they want a big tent party. Some are calling for her to be expelled. Is there room in the Democratic party for someone like Haley Stevens?

Abdul El-Sayed:

Well, when you self-expel, at some point, you're choosing to walk all the way out of the tent. And that was a choice she made.

Amna Nawaz:

And yet, your party has not yet reached consensus on this big issue of U.S. support for Israel. It was a big issue during your primary. Continues to divide many Democrats. Do you need to reach some kind of consensus to be legislatively united?

Abdul El-Sayed:

Tell you this, the public has pretty much clearly reached consensus. We don't pay our tax dollars to buy bombs and tanks for other countries. We want to pay our tax dollars to buy good schools and healthcare here on our own. Whether or not parties recognize that, that is their choice. I think that for us, we should be conditional, right, when it comes to any foreign military aid on upholding international law. So why would we send our money to a country that is absolutely destroying, making a mockery out of international law, whether it's genocide or apartheid or it is a war we have no business fighting for the annexation of a different country. If any other country behaved that way, we would think very differently about calling them an ally. I think it's our responsibility for us to just go where our principles say we ought to go and treat everybody similarly. And I'll say the same thing. I don't pay my tax dollars so the government of Egypt gets tanks or the government of Pakistan or the government of Saudi Arabia. I don't believe that we should be doing unconditional foreign military aid as a matter of course.

Amna Nawaz:

The last time you and I talked was several years ago. You were running for governor of Michigan back then and you were just about to become a father for the first time. Your daughter was, I think, days before she was born. You've seen since then anti-Muslim sentiment continue to rise in this country and it showed up in attacks against you in this election cycle. Your eldest daughter in particular, now she's old enough to see that and to hear that. And I just wonder what you and your wife tell her and talk to her about.

Abdul El-Sayed:

Well, you know, Sara is the real hero of this whole campaign.

Amna Nawaz:

And that's your wife.

Abdul El-Sayed:

My wife Sara, and she and I, when we kicked off this campaign, it was a real commitment to us that any of the strife that would come with this that we would do all we could to protect the girls from it. So there were rules around when the TV could be on uh so that they wouldn't be hit with one of those ugly commercials. We tried to narrate the experience for them so that they had an understanding of what was done. And my goal of this was that this was something that they would experience in a blunted way in you know in real time and then read about someday in real time -- or afterwards. And the hard part for me really throughout this whole thing was talking to friends and folks in the community who said how I explain this to my kids what I'm seeing out there. And the answer I'd always say is the story's not yet done. You know, if you watch a thriller, um, sometimes in the middle of the thriller, it looks like the bad guys is going to win. And, you know, as I said in in in my victory speech, the bad guys lost. And that's because I took a bet on Michigan. I didn't take a bet on me. I took a bet on Michigan. Michiganers are good people. They are open-minded. They're big-hearted. They care less about how you pray than than what you pray for. And I had 19 months of traveling up and down my state, meeting people who had never met somebody of my faith before, who are less interested in talking about faith and our differences than using our differences and an opportunity to talk about what we share together. That's human nature and human instinct. And there's always a few small-minded people who want to make America small like them. But America always responds and reminds us just how big America is. And that's a real gift. And so, you know, as we talk about this, it is important to me that all of those families out there of children who've been told they don't belong for some reason or another, not necessarily because they share my faith or because maybe they they love a different way, they they look a different way, a color of their skin, or they're just being picked on by somebody, that they remember that in the end, the good in people wins out. And we are big, we are inclusive, uh, and we're stronger because of that. And I'm just so proud of my state for having made that argument, once again.

Amna Nawaz:

It's Democratic senator elect from Michigan, Abdul El-Sayed, joining us here today.

Abdul El-Sayed:

Thank you for your time, Amna. Thanks for having me.

title: Service is not a profession but a responsibility towards society: RSS chief Mohan Bhagwat
full_text:
Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS) chief Mohan Bhagwat on Friday (November 13, 2026) said compassion and sensitivity are the foundations of humanity and society, stressing that people should serve others without expecting anything in return.

“Service is not a profession but a responsibility towards society. We do not work merely to earn our livelihood but to ensure that the world continues to function well,” Mr. Bhagwat said in an address after presenting the ‘Vidarbha Gaurav’ award to Dr. Sanjay Paithankar.

Emphasising the importance of sensitivity, Mr. Bhagwat said helping someone in distress, irrespective of whether one has a personal relationship with them, is a natural expression of humanity.

“Whether we have any relationship with a person or not, if someone somewhere is suffering, we should do whatever we can to alleviate that suffering. And while doing so, we should not feel that we are doing something extraordinary. This is a sign of humanity,” he said.

The RSS chief said awards were not given to people to motivate them to begin serving society, as those honoured had not worked with the expectation of receiving recognition.

“An award is given to honour their work and to encourage them to take it forward. The word ‘puraskar’ itself means to take something forward,” he said.

He explained that the word also meant a reward and encouragement, adding that recognising people engaged in social service was a way of appreciating their contribution and inspiring others.

Mr. Bhagwat said compassion was an expression of human sensitivity and that society survived on this sensitivity rather than merely on economic prosperity.

“Society survives on compassion and sensitivity. If this sensitivity remains alive, society will survive. If it disappears, humanity itself will be lost,” he said.

He said people often faced difficult circumstances, and their struggles could sometimes suppress their sensitivity. However, preserving compassion despite hardships was what made a person truly human.

“Whether a person is struggling with poverty or living in prosperity is not the question. What matters is what values they have preserved while living,” he said.

Mr. Bhagwat said the Indian understanding of work was different from the idea of a profession pursued merely for earning money. People should follow their respective occupations and fulfil family responsibilities while also contributing to society.

“Earning one’s livelihood is only a by-product of the work we do. The real purpose is to serve society,” he said.

He said the concept of ‘dharma’ was tied to humanity and brotherhood, and its essential characteristics were truth, compassion, purity and self-discipline.

“Humanity itself is dharma. Brotherhood is dharma,” he said.

The chief said people should live with the awareness that the divine exists within themselves and others, which would naturally create a sense of belonging and compassion.

He narrated an anecdote about a disciple who returned without eating a fruit after being asked by his teacher to consume it at a place where nobody could see him. The disciple said he could not find such a place because he believed God was present everywhere, including within himself.

Bhagwat said this awareness created a bond with others and encouraged people to serve without expecting any benefit.

title: Reframing compliance from institutional burden to student protection
summary:
Compliance has become a byword for stress for many UK universities. But doing your due diligence has added benefits for students, write Ewa Borkowska and Sandy Bhangal.

The post Reframing compliance from institutional burden to student protection appeared first on The PIE News.
full_text:
Most staff outside a university’s international office couldn’t tell you what a sponsor licence is. That’s not a criticism. Until you work with it, there’s no reason you’d know.

But the conversation changes quickly once you explain what’s at stake. Without a licence, a university can’t sponsor international students.

For institutions that rely heavily on international fees to balance their budgets, that is a serious financial threat, not an administrative detail.

The numbers tell part of the story but not the whole one

The Basic Compliance Assessment (BCA) looks at three numbers: visa refusal rate, enrolment rate and course completion rate. Assessments requested from June 1, 2026 are held to tougher thresholds.

Refusals now have to stay under 5%, half the old 10% limit, and the enrolment requirement has gone up from 90% to 95%. Completion stays at 85% for now, rising to 90% from June 2027.

Recent sector reporting suggests a lot of institutions are sitting uncomfortably close to those lines, and that the gap between them is widening depending on where they recruit from. One analysis predicts the Russell Group will be the only mission group rated green.

The point we want to make isn’t really about the figures, though. It’s that no single office controls any of them.

Refusal rates depend on who an institution recruits and how well their applications are prepared. That sits with recruitment and admissions as much as with compliance. Enrolment depends on whether courses, timetables and academic pathways are ready when a student’s visa comes through, which is down to academic departments and registry.

Each of the three metrics UKVI uses is the end result of decisions made across half a dozen teams

Completion depends on engagement monitoring, academic support and how early someone notices a student is struggling, so IT systems, personal tutors and student services all play a part.

Compliance teams sit in the middle, watching numbers that colleagues elsewhere are shaping every day, usually without realising it. So, when we say compliance is interdisciplinary, we mean it literally.

Each of the three metrics UKVI uses is the end result of decisions made across half a dozen teams.

An application an admissions officer could have queried. A timetabling clash that held up enrolment. A pastoral check-in that came too late. If compliance is treated as one office’s responsibility, that office ends up answerable for outcomes it has no means of controlling.

Students first: duty of care as the compass for recruitment, admissions and compliance

We’d rather not make this purely a story about risk, either. Doing compliance properly has benefits most universities want anyway and at the centre of all of it are students.

Engagement monitoring exists to meet sponsor duties, but it also tells you who’s turning up, and a student who’s turning up has a chance to build the connections that help them stay. The 20-hour term-time cap on work is framed as a compliance safeguard, but it also protects time for study. Quite often, compliance and a good student experience are the same thing described in different language.

That’s worth saying out loud when a compliance request lands on a team that already feels stretched. We all have a duty of care to ensure prospective students are genuine, can comply with the Immigration Rules, and are supported to enrol, comply with their conditions of leave, and see their course through to completion.

Keeping students at the heart of recruitment, admissions and compliance means:

Designing recruitment and credibility checks that protect students from unsuitable courses and unsustainable visa risk, not just protecting the licence.

Building admissions processes that are clear, timely and supportive, so students aren’t caught out by avoidable refusals or delays.

Using attendance and engagement data to reach out early, not just to report late.

Framing work-hour limits, progression requirements and reporting duties as part of a wider promise to help students succeed, not just as rules to enforce.

When we centre students, compliance stops feeling like a box-ticking exercise and starts looking like the infrastructure of a good student journey.

If the work is shared, the structure needs to reflect that

Two things help.

The first is a responsibilities map. Write down which department owns which part of the compliance lifecycle: who checks genuineness at the point of recruitment, who flags an attendance concern before it becomes an enrolment problem, who escalates a near miss and to whom. Once that’s written down and agreed, “compliance is everyone’s responsibility” stops being a slogan and becomes something people can be held to.

The second is governance that keeps up. Heads of department and senior managers need to be talking about this regularly, not only when something has gone wrong: what’s working, what isn’t, and where risk is building before it shows in the metrics.

Adding compliance to forums that already exist tends to work better than setting up another meeting nobody has time for. Departments should also be able to see their own contribution to the numbers, through a shared dashboard for example, rather than the data sitting in one office where nobody else has a reason to look.

Compliance teams don’t always have a clear, current view of their own figures either. Sponsors don’t submit numbers for the BCA; they confirm the date UKVI should calculate from and hope their own tracking lines up.

We’re not suggesting every member of staff should become a compliance officer. But keeping the licence is no longer something one department can manage on its own

There can also be a lag between a visa decision and the sponsor hearing about it. That’s a genuine operational headache, and strengthens the case for sharing the data. If the team closest to it can’t see the whole picture alone, the answer is to build that picture with the departments generating the numbers.

We’re not suggesting every member of staff should become a compliance officer. But keeping the licence is no longer something one department can manage on its own.

Institutions that map responsibilities, govern them properly and make the data visible will be better placed to get through a difficult recruitment cycle and, more importantly, to keep students safe, supported and successful along the way. Those that don’t may find out how much depends on a set of numbers most of their staff have never heard of and how quickly that can affect the students who trusted them to deliver a quality UK education experience.

Keeping the sponsor licence is everyone’s job, whether they know it or not. And at the heart of that job is a simple, shared responsibility: to treat every international student as a person we are here to support, not just a data point in a compliance metric.

title: Beyond the Grade: Turning Feedback Into Teaching With the IDE CARES Model
summary:
A student once told me that after reading my feedback, she turned to her husband and said, “Ide cares.” That comment stayed with me. It was kind, of course, but it also captured something I had been trying to do in my courses for years: hold students to meaningful academic and professional standards while making […]

The post Beyond the Grade: Turning Feedback Into Teaching With the IDE CARES Model appeared first on Faculty Focus | Higher Ed Teaching & Learning.
full_text:
A student once told me that after reading my feedback, she turned to her husband and said, “Ide cares.” That comment stayed with me.

It was kind, of course, but it also captured something I had been trying to do in my courses for years: hold students to meaningful academic and professional standards while making sure they understood that my feedback was meant to help them grow, not simply explain why they lost points.

That moment eventually led me to name the feedback approach I had already been using: the IDE CARES Feedback Model. The model is designed for faculty who want feedback that goes beyond justifying a grade. It helps students understand what they did well, where they need to improve, why the standard matters, and how to carry the feedback into their next submission.

I developed the model in health administration courses, but the structure can work in many settings, especially online, hybrid, writing-intensive, or accelerated courses where written feedback may be the main one-on-one teaching students receive.

Why Feedback Needs More Structure

Many of us were taught some version of the “feedback sandwich”: begin with something positive, address what needs improvement, and close with encouragement. That structure can be helpful, but on its own, it is not always enough.

Students may appreciate the positive tone but still leave unsure what to revise. They may see a rubric score but not understand how their work missed the standard. They may read “APA needs work” or “analysis needs more depth” and not know what those comments actually require them to do next.

Recent feedback research points to a practical reality many faculty already see: feedback only helps when students understand it and know what to do next. Williams (2024) describes effective feedback as a contributor to student motivation, learning, and performance, while also noting that feedback practices can be difficult to deliver well. Dawson et al. (2024) focus on what students actually do with feedback, including how they seek it, make sense of it, use it, and manage their response to it. For instructors, the takeaway is straightforward: feedback should be clear, usable, and connected to the next attempt. That is where IDE CARES comes in.

I: Identify Strengths and Growth Areas

Start by naming what the student did well and where growth is needed. This should be specific, not generic.

Instead of writing, “Good job,” try:

“You selected a relevant topic and clearly understand why this issue matters in practice. The next step is to strengthen the paper by connecting your major claims to scholarly or authoritative sources.”

This opening does two things. It shows the student that you actually read the work, and it frames correction as part of growth rather than punishment.

D: Direct Students Back to the Rubric and Assignment Directions

Students can take grading personally when they cannot see how the comments connect to the assignment expectations. Directing students back to the rubric helps them see that the feedback is tied to criteria, not instructor preference.

For example:

“The rubric requires evidence-supported analysis. Right now, the paper includes a reference page, but the body paragraphs do not include in-text citations showing where source information was used.”

That type of comment is much more useful than “Needs citations.” It tells the student what standard was missed and where to look.

E: Explain Why the Standard Matters

Students are more likely to use feedback when they understand why the issue matters beyond the assignment.

In my courses, I often explain that APA, citation use, professional tone, and evidence-based reasoning are not just academic requirements. They are workplace skills. Future professionals need to document decisions, support recommendations, and communicate clearly with supervisors, colleagues, patients, clients, or community partners.

A feedback comment might say:

“In-text citations are important because they allow the reader to verify the evidence behind your claims. In professional settings, unsupported recommendations can weaken credibility and decision-making.”

This helps students understand that the standard is not just my preference. It is part of the professional skill set they are building.

C: Clarify the Correction Needed

Vague feedback rarely leads to strong revision. Students need to know what to do.

Instead of writing, “Expand this section,” try:

“To strengthen this section, add one current scholarly or authoritative source, explain how it supports your point, and connect the evidence back to the assignment question.”

Instead of “Improve discussion replies,” try:

“In your next reply, directly reference one point your peer made, add a new idea or example, and ask a question that moves the discussion forward.”

Clarifying the correction turns feedback into a next step.

A: Apply Feedback Through Revision or Resubmission Opportunities

This is one of the most important parts of the model. Feedback should not always be the endpoint of learning.

When course policy allows, I invite students to revise or resubmit lower-scoring assignments after reviewing my feedback. I frame this as an opportunity, not a requirement and not a punishment. The message is simple: detailed feedback is most valuable when students are allowed to use it.

A practical resubmission note might read:

“You are welcome to revise and resubmit this assignment after reviewing the feedback. Focus first on adding in-text citations to each major body paragraph, strengthening the analysis section, and correcting the reference page format.”

Faculty should be clear about deadlines, eligibility, and grading limits. But when possible, revision gives students a chance to demonstrate learning rather than simply move on with a low score.

R: Reinforce Confidence While Maintaining Standards

Supportive feedback should not erase expectations. Students need encouragement, but they also need to know the standard still matters.

For example:

“You have a strong topic and a clear interest in this issue. To reach the next level, the paper needs stronger source integration and closer alignment with the assignment criteria.”

This type of feedback communicates belief in the student while preserving rigor. It avoids two extremes: harsh comments that discourage students and overly soft comments that do not lead to improvement.

E: Encourage Questions and Support-Seeking

Students may not know how to interpret feedback on their own. Invite them into the process.

A simple sentence can help:

“Please reach out if you would like help applying this feedback before your next submission.”

You can also direct students to writing centers, library support, APA resources, office hours, sample papers, recorded walkthroughs, or course announcements. In online courses especially, students may need repeated reminders that asking for clarification is part of learning.

S: Support Continued Professional Growth

Close by connecting the feedback to who the student is becoming.

In a healthcare course, I might write:

“As you continue preparing for healthcare leadership roles, the ability to support recommendations with credible evidence will strengthen your professional communication and decision-making.”

In another discipline, the wording may change, but the purpose is the same. Students should understand that writing, reasoning, revision, evidence use, and professional communication are not just classroom tasks. They are transferable skills.

Using IDE CARES in Discussions and Assignments

For written assignments, I often begin with a short overall comment, then move criterion by criterion through the rubric. Under each criterion, I identify what worked, explain what limited the score, and give a clear action step. I usually end with two or three priorities for revision or the next assignment.

For discussions, I use the same model in a shorter form. I might acknowledge a student’s relevant point, direct them back to the expectation for evidence or peer engagement, clarify what a stronger reply would include, and encourage them to ask a question or bring in a specific example next time.

This approach also works well for class-wide feedback. If several students miss the same expectation, I post an announcement or short walkthrough before the next assignment. That saves time and helps students see common patterns.

Making Feedback Manageable

Detailed feedback takes time, but it can be made more sustainable. I recommend creating a feedback bank organized by common rubric areas: content, analysis, source use, APA, organization, discussion engagement, and professionalism. Then personalize each comment with at least one detail from the student’s actual submission.

A “next steps” section also helps. Students do not always need ten things to fix at once. They need to know which two or three changes matter most.

The goal is not to write more feedback for the sake of writing more. The goal is to write feedback students can actually use.

Feedback is Teaching

Feedback should not merely explain a grade after learning is over. It should help students keep learning.

The IDE CARES model gives faculty a practical way to make feedback specific, compassionate, rigorous, and actionable. It reminds students that we see their effort, that standards matter, and that improvement is possible.

When feedback is done well, students do not just learn what they got wrong. They learn how to revise, how to think more deeply, how to communicate more professionally, and how to carry those skills into the next assignment and beyond.

That is the kind of feedback students remember. More importantly, it is the kind they can use.

Dr. Dawn Ide is a healthcare administration educator and curriculum developer with more than 15 years of experience teaching across face-to-face, hybrid, and online postsecondary settings. Her work focuses on healthcare administration education, online learning, assessment design, academic integrity, and workforce preparation.

References

Dawson, P., Yan, Z., Lipnevich, A., Tai, J., Boud, D., & Mahoney, P. (2024). Measuring what learners do in feedback: The feedback literacy behaviour scale. Assessment & Evaluation in Higher Education, 49(3), 348–362. https://doi.org/10.1080/02602938.2023.2240983
